    UMAP, densMAP, PaCMAP, LocalMAP, ForceAtlas2 and NCVis¶

    Python port of the R vignettes UMAP, densMAP and den-SNE, PaCMAP and ForceAtlas2. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    The graph layout family. UMAP and its density-preserving sibling densMAP, PaCMAP and its locally adjusted successor LocalMAP, Gephi's ForceAtlas2 and NCVis. All of them start from a kNN graph and pull neighbours together while pushing everything else apart. Where they differ is in what they push and when.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import time
import warnings

# umap-learn's spectral init on the disconnected cluster graph and tqdm in a
# headless kernel both warn; neither matters here. Set before the imports, which
# is when tqdm warns.
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Graph is not fully connected")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="IProgress not found")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pacmap
import polars as pl
import umap
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

import manifolds_rs as mf

pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(60)


def scatter(
    ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks."""
    ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])


def panels(
    embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False
    )
    for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True):
        scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap)
    fig.tight_layout()


def timed(fn) -> float:
    """Wall time of one call, in seconds."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    return time.perf_counter() - start

    UMAP¶

    UMAP builds a weighted kNN graph in the input space, where the edge weights say how likely two points are to be connected under a local, adaptive metric (the kNN vignette has the searches). It then minimises the cross-entropy between that graph and its low-dimensional twin, pulling connected points together and pushing unconnected ones apart. That is why UMAP is great at clusters: if two points are unlikely neighbours, the repulsion drives them apart and you get clean separation.

    The flip side: UMAP has no incentive to keep relative distances along a continuum. On trajectory-like data the loss treats weakly connected distant points as things to repel, not as part of one structure, and continuous manifolds get torn into spurious clusters. UMAP is a visualisation tool, not a metric space!

    The default optimiser is a parallel Adam, the same idea as uwot::umap2(). Each node gathers its gradient and takes its Adam step in one pass, in parallel, so it scales with your cores and the same seed gives the same embedding every time.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    X_clust, y_clust = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000)
X_swiss, t_swiss = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(1_000)
X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000)
order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_traj))
    X_clust, y_clust = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000) X_swiss, t_swiss = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(1_000) X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000) order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_traj))

    Clusters: UMAP pulls apart what PCA leaves overlapping. Swiss roll and trajectory: PCA shows you the continuum, UMAP breaks it into pieces with some bleeding in between. Pick the algorithm for the structure you expect.

    Pre-computed kNN graphs¶

    Sweeping min_dist with the neighbours fixed? Build the graph once and pass it to fit_transform.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    idx15, dist15 = mf.knn_graph(X_clust, k=15, ann="nndescent")

panels(
    {
        f"min_dist = {md}": mf.UMAP(min_dist=md).fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15
        )
        for md in (0.05, 0.5, 1.0)
    },
    y_clust,
)
    idx15, dist15 = mf.knn_graph(X_clust, k=15, ann="nndescent") panels( { f"min_dist = {md}": mf.UMAP(min_dist=md).fit_transform( X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15 ) for md in (0.05, 0.5, 1.0) }, y_clust, )

    Optimisers¶

    Five of them:

    • "adam_parallel" (default): parallel Adam, reproducible.
    • "adam": the same Adam, single-threaded.
    • "sgd": the classic umap-learn and uwot::umap() SGD with edge sampling. Single-threaded, reproducible.
    • "sgd_parallel": the same SGD lock-free, Hogwild! style. All threads write to the embedding without locks, which is where the speed comes from. The price: with more than one thread it is not reproducible run to run, seed or no seed.
    • "adam_v06": the Adam of umap-learn 0.6, with its own learning rate schedule. Pair it with init="recursive", the umap-learn 0.6 label propagation initialisation, and it takes the short warm-up umap-learn uses for a good start.

    Like umap-learn, the SGD optimisers drop to 200 epochs above 10k samples unless you set n_epochs.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    optimisers = {
    "adam_parallel": mf.UMAP(),
    "sgd": mf.UMAP(optimiser="sgd"),
    "sgd_parallel": mf.UMAP(optimiser="sgd_parallel"),
    "adam_v06 + recursive": mf.UMAP(optimiser="adam_v06", init="recursive"),
}
panels(
    {
        name: est.fit_transform(X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15)
        for name, est in optimisers.items()
    },
    y_clust,
)
    optimisers = { "adam_parallel": mf.UMAP(), "sgd": mf.UMAP(optimiser="sgd"), "sgd_parallel": mf.UMAP(optimiser="sgd_parallel"), "adam_v06 + recursive": mf.UMAP(optimiser="adam_v06", init="recursive"), } panels( { name: est.fit_transform(X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15) for name, est in optimisers.items() }, y_clust, )

    Same clusters four times. The 0.6 Adam with the recursive start lands on a different arrangement, which is the initialisation talking, not the optimiser. On reproducibility, don't take my word for it:

    name: np.array_equal(
        mf.UMAP(optimiser=name).fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15
        ),
        mf.UMAP(optimiser=name).fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15
        ),
    )
    for name in ("adam_parallel", "sgd_parallel")
}

    densMAP¶

    Cluster sizes in a UMAP mean nothing. A blob twice as wide as its neighbour might be ten times tighter in the input, because nothing in the loss cares how spread out a neighbourhood was. densMAP adds one term:

    \[-\lambda \cdot \mathrm{Corr}(\log R_o, \log R_e)\]

    \(R_o\) is a local radius in the input, a graph-weighted average squared distance to a point's neighbours, and \(R_e\) the matching radius in the embedding. Maximise the correlation and a tight cluster stays tight, a diffuse one diffuse. Same graph, same repulsion, same optimisers otherwise. The knobs:

    • lambda_: weight of the density term, 2.0 by default. 0 gives plain UMAP back.
    • DensParams(frac=...): fraction of the epochs, at the end, over which the term runs. 0.3 by default; switching it on from epoch zero fights the initialisation. Over the last 30% only, so you pay maybe a third more wall time.
    • DensParams(var_shift=...): a shift on the variance of the embedding log-radii that keeps the correlation sane when the radii collapse.

    The umap-learn 0.6 Adam has no density term, so densMAP refuses "adam_v06".

    To see any of this we need local density before and after. A proxy for \(R_o\): the log of the mean squared distance to the 15 nearest neighbours.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    def local_radii(x: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> np.ndarray:
    """Log mean squared distance to the `k` nearest neighbours, per point."""
    _, d = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="kmknn")
    return np.log((d.astype(np.float64) ** 2).mean(axis=1) + 1e-8)


def dens_cor(radii: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Spearman correlation of input and embedding local radii."""
    return round(float(spearmanr(radii, local_radii(emb)).statistic), 3)


X_dens, y_dens = mf.datasets.clustered(10_000, n_clusters=8)
radii = local_radii(X_dens)

dens = {
    "UMAP": mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X_dens),
    "densMAP": mf.DensMAP().fit_transform(X_dens),
}
panels(dens, radii, cmap="viridis")
pl.DataFrame({"method": list(dens), "rho": [dens_cor(radii, e) for e in dens.values()]})

    Coloured by the input radius. UMAP hands you clusters of roughly equal size whatever the colour. densMAP lets the diffuse ones sprawl and squeezes the tight ones, and the Spearman correlation rho puts a number on it.

    lambda_=0 is plain UMAP, bit for bit. A handy sanity check, and the cheapest way to A/B the thing:

    In [10]:
    Copied!

    np.array_equal(mf.DensMAP(lambda_=0.0).fit_transform(X_dens), dens["UMAP"])

    Density along a manifold¶

    Clusters are the easy case. The biased swiss roll samples non-uniformly along the roll, so the density gradient is continuous rather than blocky.

radii_bias = local_radii(X_bias)

bias = {
    "UMAP": mf.UMAP(ann="exhaustive").fit_transform(X_bias),
    "densMAP": mf.DensMAP(ann="exhaustive").fit_transform(X_bias),
}
panels(bias, radii_bias, cmap="viridis")
pl.DataFrame(
    {"method": list(bias), "rho": [dens_cor(radii_bias, e) for e in bias.values()]}

    Tuning lambda¶

    The usual framing is that lambda_ trades cluster separation for density fidelity. Let's check on 2000 points. Separation here is the mean distance between cluster centroids over the mean distance of a point to its own centroid.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    def separation(emb: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Mean centroid distance over mean within-cluster distance to the centroid."""
    ids = np.unique(labels)
    cent = np.stack([emb[labels == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids])
    within = np.mean(
        [
            np.linalg.norm(emb[labels == g] - cent[i], axis=1).mean()
            for i, g in enumerate(ids)
        ]
    )
    return float(pdist(cent).mean() / within)


X_small, y_small = mf.datasets.clustered(2_000, n_clusters=8)
radii_small = local_radii(X_small)
idx_small, dist_small = mf.knn_graph(X_small, k=15)

rows = []
for lam in (0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0):
    emb = mf.DensMAP(lambda_=lam).fit_transform(
        X_small, knn_indices=idx_small, knn_distances=dist_small
    )
    rows.append(
        {
            "lambda": lam,
            "rho": dens_cor(radii_small, emb),
            "separation": round(separation(emb, y_small), 2),
        }
    )
pl.DataFrame(rows)
    def separation(emb: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float: """Mean centroid distance over mean within-cluster distance to the centroid.""" ids = np.unique(labels) cent = np.stack([emb[labels == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids]) within = np.mean( [ np.linalg.norm(emb[labels == g] - cent[i], axis=1).mean() for i, g in enumerate(ids) ] ) return float(pdist(cent).mean() / within) X_small, y_small = mf.datasets.clustered(2_000, n_clusters=8) radii_small = local_radii(X_small) idx_small, dist_small = mf.knn_graph(X_small, k=15) rows = [] for lam in (0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0): emb = mf.DensMAP(lambda_=lam).fit_transform( X_small, knn_indices=idx_small, knn_distances=dist_small ) rows.append( { "lambda": lam, "rho": dens_cor(radii_small, emb), "separation": round(separation(emb, y_small), 2), } ) pl.DataFrame(rows)

    lambdarhoseparation
    f64f64f64
    0.00.01119.22
    0.50.88926.06
    2.00.9326.38
    5.00.93824.07

    Not quite what the framing promises. Nearly all the fidelity arrives by lambda_ = 0.5 and barely moves after. Separation improves over plain UMAP the moment the density term switches on, peaks early and then erodes slowly; only at 10 does it drop back to the 0 baseline. So on this data the trade-off only bites well past the default. Well-separated blobs are the friendly case, so sweep on your own data, but 2.0 sits on the flat part of both curves and is a sane start.

    PaCMAP¶

    PaCMAP builds its embedding from three kinds of pair. Near pairs keep local neighbourhoods. Mid-near pairs, the second closest of six random points, are a medium-range pull that anchors the global structure. Further pairs, random distant points minus the near pairs, push.

    The trick is the phased schedule. In phase one the mid-near weight decays from 1000 to 3, which pulls points into a globally coherent arrangement before any local structure is resolved. In phase two it holds at 3 while the near weight rises, so local structure emerges without wrecking the layout. Phase three runs on near and further pairs only. UMAP optimises one objective from the start; PaCMAP settles the global picture first.

    Three things to know:

    • PCA initialisation. Random init throws away most of the global structure, hence init="pca" by default.
    • n_near is less touchy than UMAP's n_neighbors. The paper's 10 works across a wide range of data. The search runs n_near + 50 wide and the near pairs are the best of those by locally scaled distance, so a pre-computed graph should be n_near + 50 wide too.
    • Mid-near pairs don't come from the graph. They are sampled.

    LocalMAP¶

    LocalMAP is PaCMAP with a different phase three. Further pairs that already sit more than max_distance apart in the embedding get resampled (they have done their job), and the near-pair forces are scaled by their embedding distance. The upshot: clusters PaCMAP leaves touching get pulled apart, and the global arrangement from the first two phases stays. Same arguments as PaCMAP, plus max_distance (default 10).

    The hierarchical data is where the difference between UMAP and the PaCMAP family shows. 16 subclusters in 4 supergroups, in 50 dimensions.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    X_hier, supergroup, subgroup = mf.datasets.hierarchical(10_000, n_subclusters=4)

hier = {
    "UMAP": mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X_hier),
    "PaCMAP": mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform(X_hier),
    "LocalMAP": mf.LocalMAP().fit_transform(X_hier),
}
panels(hier, supergroup)
    X_hier, supergroup, subgroup = mf.datasets.hierarchical(10_000, n_subclusters=4) hier = { "UMAP": mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X_hier), "PaCMAP": mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform(X_hier), "LocalMAP": mf.LocalMAP().fit_transform(X_hier), } panels(hier, supergroup)

    Coloured by supergroup. Two numbers per embedding: the Spearman correlation of subcluster centroid distances, input against embedding (global), and the fraction of each point's 15 nearest neighbours that survive (local).

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    def global_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, groups: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Spearman correlation of group centroid distances, input vs embedding."""
    ids = np.unique(groups)
    cx = np.stack([x[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids])
    ce = np.stack([emb[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids])
    return float(spearmanr(pdist(cx), pdist(ce)).statistic)


def knn_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> float:
    """Mean fraction of each point's `k` exact neighbours kept in the embedding."""
    a, _ = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="exhaustive")
    b, _ = mf.knn_graph(emb, k=k, ann="exhaustive")
    return sum(len(set(i) & set(j)) for i, j in zip(a, b, strict=True)) / a.size


pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "method": list(hier),
        "global": [global_preservation(X_hier, e, subgroup) for e in hier.values()],
        "local": [knn_preservation(X_hier, e) for e in hier.values()],
        "separation": [separation(e, subgroup) for e in hier.values()],
    }
).with_columns(pl.exclude("method").round(3))
    def global_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, groups: np.ndarray) -> float: """Spearman correlation of group centroid distances, input vs embedding.""" ids = np.unique(groups) cx = np.stack([x[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids]) ce = np.stack([emb[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids]) return float(spearmanr(pdist(cx), pdist(ce)).statistic) def knn_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> float: """Mean fraction of each point's `k` exact neighbours kept in the embedding.""" a, _ = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="exhaustive") b, _ = mf.knn_graph(emb, k=k, ann="exhaustive") return sum(len(set(i) & set(j)) for i, j in zip(a, b, strict=True)) / a.size pl.DataFrame( { "method": list(hier), "global": [global_preservation(X_hier, e, subgroup) for e in hier.values()], "local": [knn_preservation(X_hier, e) for e in hier.values()], "separation": [separation(e, subgroup) for e in hier.values()], } ).with_columns(pl.exclude("method").round(3))
    Out[14]:
    shape: (3, 4)
    methodgloballocalseparation
    strf64f64f64
    "UMAP"0.5520.04843.589
    "PaCMAP"0.7290.04991.266
    "LocalMAP"0.7150.07725.182

    separation is the score from the densMAP section, over the 16 subclusters.

    PaCMAP places the supergroups better than UMAP (global) and squeezes every subcluster into a dot, hence its huge separation score. LocalMAP keeps the global placement and gives the subclusters their internal spread back: more of each point's neighbours survive (local), and the subclusters get bigger relative to the gaps, so its separation score drops. Don't read the score as "worse": dots are easy to separate and tell you nothing about what is inside them.

    {
        "PaCMAP": mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform(X_traj)[order],
        "LocalMAP": mf.LocalMAP().fit_transform(X_traj)[order],
    },
    y_traj[order],
)
    panels( { "PaCMAP": mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform(X_traj)[order], "LocalMAP": mf.LocalMAP().fit_transform(X_traj)[order], }, y_traj[order], )

    On the swiss roll both keep the gradient along the roll. On the trajectory LocalMAP does what it was built for and pulls apart what touches, which on a continuum means tearing the branches into islands. The reference pacmap implementation of LocalMAP does the same on this data. For trajectories stay with PaCMAP, or better, PHATE.

    Pre-computed kNN and the phase schedule¶

    With the graph fixed you can play with the schedule. Here phase one runs to epoch 300 instead of 100, so the mid-near pairs dominate for much longer.

panels(

            X_hier, knn_indices=idx60, knn_distances=dist60
        ),
        "phase 1 to epoch 300": mf.PaCMAP(
            optim_params=mf.PacmapOptim(phase1_end=300, phase2_end=400)
        ).fit_transform(X_hier, knn_indices=idx60, knn_distances=dist60),
    },
    supergroup,
)
    idx60, dist60 = mf.knn_graph(X_hier, k=60, ann="ivf") panels( { "default schedule": mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform( X_hier, knn_indices=idx60, knn_distances=dist60 ), "phase 1 to epoch 300": mf.PaCMAP( optim_params=mf.PacmapOptim(phase1_end=300, phase2_end=400) ).fit_transform(X_hier, knn_indices=idx60, knn_distances=dist60), }, supergroup, )

    ForceAtlas2¶

    Gephi's force-directed layout, known in single cell from scanpy's draw_graph and PAGA-initialised layouts. ForceAtlas2 treats the graph as a physical system. Every node repels every other with a force of 1/d, scaled by the node masses (1 + degree, so hubs push harder). Every edge pulls its ends together, linearly with distance or logarithmically with lin_log=True. Gravity pulls everything to the origin so disconnected components don't drift off. Step sizes follow Gephi's adaptive speed, and the all-pairs repulsion runs on a Barnes-Hut tree.

    How is that different from UMAP? UMAP samples edges and negatives and minimises a loss. ForceAtlas2 visits every edge every epoch and has no loss, just forces. No min_dist or spread either: the scale of the layout falls out of scaling_ratio (repulsion) against the edge weights (attraction). It runs on the same fuzzy union graph UMAP builds, as scanpy does, and needs it symmetric, so UmapGraph(mix_weight=...) has to stay at 1.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {
        "UMAP": mf.UMAP().fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15
        ),
        "ForceAtlas2": mf.ForceAtlas2().fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15
        ),
        "ForceAtlas2, LinLog": mf.ForceAtlas2(lin_log=True).fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15
        ),
    },
    y_clust,
)
    panels( { "UMAP": mf.UMAP().fit_transform( X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15 ), "ForceAtlas2": mf.ForceAtlas2().fit_transform( X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15 ), "ForceAtlas2, LinLog": mf.ForceAtlas2(lin_log=True).fit_transform( X_clust, knn_indices=idx15, knn_distances=dist15 ), }, y_clust, )

    Same global arrangement as UMAP, since both start from the same spectral initialisation. With linear attraction and a dense within-cluster graph, ForceAtlas2 crushes each cluster into a tight blob. LinLog's logarithmic attraction grows much slower with distance, so the clusters open up again. The coordinates live on Gephi's scale, so tens of thousands are normal; only the relative positions mean anything.

    Trajectories are where force-directed layouts get used most in single cell.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {"ForceAtlas2": mf.ForceAtlas2().fit_transform(X_traj)[order]},
    y_traj[order],
)
    panels( {"ForceAtlas2": mf.ForceAtlas2().fit_transform(X_traj)[order]}, y_traj[order], )

    The knobs worth knowing: scaling_ratio (repulsion, bigger spreads everything), gravity (raise it if small components float away, lower it if everything gets squashed into a ball), lin_log, n_epochs (no learning rate to anneal, so more epochs is a more settled layout), and Fa2Optim(dissuade_hubs=True), which pushes hubs to the edge of their community. Leave theta and jitter_tolerance alone unless you know why you're touching them.

    NCVis¶

    NCVis (Artemenkov & Panov, 2020) swaps UMAP's cross-entropy for noise-contrastive estimation. The graph is the plain kNN graph, made undirected, with no weights at all. Each edge pulls its two points together and draws uniform negatives that push apart, each weighted by how likely the pair is data rather than noise. The normalisation constant that makes that a proper probability is learned on the side, as one more parameter. The negatives ramp up with the cube of progress, so the early epochs mostly attract and the late ones do most of the pushing.

    The defaults are Sean Pedersen's NCVis+, whose kernel this is a port of: a PCA start scaled as a whole to std 10 on its first axis, min_dist 0.001, learning rate 2, 50 epochs and on average 10 negatives per edge. The PCA start is the one that matters for global structure, and like for PaCMAP it is the default for that reason. The optimiser is hogwild, so a fixed seed reproduces only on one thread (mf.set_num_threads(1)).

    Back to the hierarchical data, against UMAP and PaCMAP.

}

    Global structure lands about where UMAP's does: the supergroups stay together, the arrangement is a bit less faithful than PaCMAP's. Local structure is the odd one out. NCVis keeps roughly twice the exact neighbours of UMAP and PaCMAP, and the clusters come out visibly tighter. Drop the PCA start and the global score collapses to nothing, with a ring of stray points that 50 epochs never pull back in. Keep the PCA start.

    The 1k swiss roll is NCVis' weak spot. With 15 neighbours on a sparse sheet it tears the roll into strips, worse than LocalMAP. More epochs, more negatives or a larger min_dist barely change that; a wider graph does. At n_neighbors=30 the sheet mostly holds together. The trajectory comes out fine: the branches are there and in the right order.

    Benchmarks¶

    Against umap-learn 0.6 and the reference PaCMAP package (which also ships LocalMAP), on all cores. One run each, wall time in seconds, neighbour search included. Both references compile with numba on first use, so they get a warm-up call on a small dataset before the clock starts.

    Like for like where it exists: umap-learn's default 0.6 path (recursive init and Adam) against our "adam_v06" with init="recursive", and its legacy SGD layout against our "sgd_parallel", which is equally non-reproducible.

    In [24]:
    Copied! 
    X_warm, _ = mf.datasets.clustered(2_000)
umap.UMAP(optimizer="adam").fit_transform(X_warm)
umap.UMAP(compatibility_layout=True).fit_transform(X_warm)
pacmap.PaCMAP().fit_transform(X_warm)
pacmap.LocalMAP().fit_transform(X_warm)


def bench(x: np.ndarray) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Wall time of our UMAP, PaCMAP, LocalMAP and NCVis and the references on `x`."""
    runs = {
        "manifolds-rs UMAP adam_parallel": lambda: mf.UMAP().fit_transform(x),
        "manifolds-rs UMAP adam_v06 + recursive": lambda: mf.UMAP(
            optimiser="adam_v06", init="recursive"
        ).fit_transform(x),
        "umap-learn adam + recursive": lambda: umap.UMAP(
            optimizer="adam"
        ).fit_transform(x),
        "manifolds-rs UMAP sgd_parallel": lambda: mf.UMAP(
            optimiser="sgd_parallel"
        ).fit_transform(x),
        "umap-learn sgd": lambda: umap.UMAP(compatibility_layout=True).fit_transform(x),
        "manifolds-rs PaCMAP": lambda: mf.PaCMAP().fit_transform(x),
        "pacmap PaCMAP": lambda: pacmap.PaCMAP().fit_transform(x),
        "manifolds-rs LocalMAP": lambda: mf.LocalMAP().fit_transform(x),
        "pacmap LocalMAP": lambda: pacmap.LocalMAP().fit_transform(x),
        "manifolds-rs NCVis": lambda: mf.NCVis().fit_transform(x),
    }
    return pl.DataFrame(
        [{"method": k, "seconds": timed(fn)} for k, fn in runs.items()]
    ).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))


bench(mf.datasets.clustered(50_000)[0])

    UMAP: against umap-learn's 0.6 default (recursive init plus Adam), our port of the same thing is several times faster, and our default parallel Adam a little faster still. On the legacy SGD the gap is smaller, but still there. PaCMAP and LocalMAP: a fraction of the reference package's time. NCVis is the slowest of ours here. The kNN search and the PCA start are a rounding error; the 50 epochs of hogwild SGD are the bill.
